newsitem.title: CANADA: Plugged In: Building a Communications Ark.
newsitem.headline: Plugged In: Building a Communications Ark.

text.p: The Old Testament's Noah did not need a modem, a personal computer or even satellite maps when he was receiving special instructions to build an Ark in preparation for the Flood.
But for lesser mortals the Internet has been a god-send after the surging Red River washed away homes, life savings and many a dream in recent weeks in Manitoba and North Dakota.

The World Wide Web became, seemingly overnight, a listening post, a depot of helpful ideas, and a lively chronicle of the disaster that was being called the flood of the century by emergency workers and others.
"Help, I am stuck in my basement and I can't get out. Help!," read one message at a site for flood victims run by Thomson New Media, at http://netreader.com.

Besides allowing for emergency messages, the forums also helped people in the flood zone and on the outside communicate with friends and family while phone lines jammed during the height of the emergency.
"Billy: could not get thru (sic) by phone, did you evacuate? We are praying for you, love Mark," read one such message.

One of the most remarkable elements of the flood was the number of volunteers, money and donations of clothing and bedding that poured into the area. The Net played a part in channeling the generosity by issuing a general call for outside help and directing people to relief agencies.

Much practical advice could also be found on the Net. The Red Cross, at www.redcross.ca, advised people to assemble an emergency kit, have a flashlight at the ready, and a vehicle with a full tank of gas.
During a flood, the agency advised:
- Keep listening to the radio for instructions and information about support services
- Evacuate immediately when instructed to do so
- Ensure electricity and gas are shut off
- Do not drive through flooded areas
- If your vehicle stalls in water, abandon it.
At one flood site, www.tetres.ca, a writer living in the U.S. noted it was only through the Internet that she could follow what was happening to her old home town.
"I was very teary-eyed to see how much my southern Manitoba had been affected by the 'Red Sea.' We don't get too much news of the actual events unless we're online, living in the southern U.S."

At the "Red River Diary," located at www.manflood.com, Net surfers were invited to follow writer Kathleen Easton and photographer Gorden Chorney as they worked on a book on the flood while they traveled around Manitoba and North Dakota.
While people could tune to television news or read newspapers to follow the tragic story of the flood, sometimes the news on the Net seemed more vital and to the point.

"This past week we've been trying to get some photos of work being done on the floodgates that protect Winnipeg," wrote Easton. "We found that the bolts were snapping off and the large, heavy steel doors were in desperate need of reinforcing."

This is not the first time the Net has a played a useful, if not life saving, role in a major crisis. In fact it now seems almost routine that sites will spring up in cyberspace when a big event is occurring. It is something people count on in times of need.
Sometimes it's easy to forget when you are inundated with banner ads, plug-ins and e-mail, that what the Net was originally all about was bringing the world a little closer together.
(For ideas or comments on the weekly Plugged In column contact: russell.blinch@reuters.com)
